sections.h2: Does Iowa tax capital gains on a house sale?
sections.html:
Not with a separate tax. Profit from selling a house is reported on your Iowa individual income tax return, and for tax year 2026 one flat rate of 3.8 percent applies to every level of taxable income.

On the Iowa return, the capital gain or loss line starts from 100 percent of the amount on your federal Form 1040. The capital gain deduction is not taken on that line, because a qualifying deduction goes on its own line. If your federal return needs Schedule D and Form 8949, a copy goes with the Iowa return.

Do not confuse two 3.8 percent figures. The Iowa rate and the federal net investment income tax share a number and nothing else. They are separate taxes with separate rules, and both can matter on a large gain.

A house that was your main home qualifies for an exclusion of up to $250,000 in gain, or up to $500,000 when you file jointly. Iowa generally follows the federal rules on excluding gain from a principal residence, so the federal exclusion also keeps that gain off your Iowa taxable income.

You have to pass two tests:

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for at least 24 months within the five years ending at the sale.
  • Use: you, and your spouse on a joint return, each used it as a main home for 24 months or more inside that same window.

The two stretches can fall in different months. Taking the exclusion on another home sale during the prior two years usually rules it out. IRS Publication 523 covers exceptions and partial exclusions.

A Form 1099-S in your mailbox means the sale gets reported, even if all of the gain is excludable. The same goes when only part of the gain can be excluded; use Form 8949 with Schedule D.

sections.h2: When the gain is bigger than the exclusion
sections.html:
Gain above the exclusion is taxed federally as a capital gain and in Iowa at the flat state rate. The federal rate depends on how long you held the property.

SituationTax treatment
Held one year or lessShort-term, taxed as ordinary income
Held more than one yearLong-term, federal rates of 0, 15 or 20 percent by taxable income
Unrecaptured section 1250 gain (depreciation on real property)Maximum federal rate of 25 percent
Iowa individual income tax, 20263.8 percent flat
Iowa interest on overdue tax, from January 1, 202610 percent a year, 0.8 percent a month

The federal net investment income tax is 3.8 percent for single filers above $200,000, joint filers above $250,000 and separate filers above $125,000 of modified adjusted gross income. It does not apply to the part of a home sale gain that is excluded as a principal residence, but gain above the exclusion can be hit.

Most Iowa capital gain deductions ended with tax year 2023. Repealed categories include gains from selling real estate used in a non-farm business, an entire business, timber, cattle, horses or breeding livestock (with an exception for retired farmers), and employer securities sold to a qualified Iowa employee stock ownership plan.

The change took effect January 1, 2023. Installment sales that began before that date still qualify for the deduction. Some older reference material for non-farm real property is still around, and the 2023 changes control.

If you read older guidance that gave a ten-year holding rule for business real estate, ignore it. A rental or commercial property sold after 2022 does not get that deduction.

  • Retired farmers aged 55 or older may still deduct gain from farm real estate if they materially participated in farming for ten years in total.
  • A retired farmer has a single lifetime election.
  • Electing the deduction blocks the beginning farmer tax credit and the farm lease income exclusion.
  • Gain from an employee-owned corporation's stock has its own phase-in: 33 percent excluded for 2023, 66 percent for 2024 and 100 percent from 2025.

A house in town or a rental house falls outside those farm rules. A principal residence relies on the federal exclusion.

An heir's tax basis usually resets to the home's fair market value at the date of death, instead of what the deceased paid. For that reason a sale soon after inheriting often leaves little or no taxable gain.

The personal representative may choose an alternate valuation date and use the value then. Without a Schedule A (Form 8971), you can fall back on the appraised value at death for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes. A home given to the decedent within one year before death can keep the decedent's adjusted basis rather than the death-date value.

Hold on to an appraisal from the date of death. It is the first paper a preparer asks for, and it is hard to recreate later.

sections.h2: Do nonresidents owe Iowa tax on a house they sell in Iowa?
sections.html:
Yes, once the Iowa-source income reaches the filing trigger. Capital gain on the sale of Iowa property counts as income from Iowa property, along with rental income. A nonresident or part-year resident must file when Iowa-source net income is $1,000 or more, unless income falls under the standard thresholds.

For the 2025 return year those thresholds were more than $9,000 for single or married filing separately filers, and more than $13,500 for joint filers, head of household and qualifying surviving spouse. Higher amounts apply to people 65 and older.

Owners who sell an Iowa house after moving away, and heirs living out of state, often miss this step. Look into it before the sale money is spent.

sections.h2: Other costs when you sell an Iowa house
sections.html:
Iowa property tax and state transfer tax are separate from any income tax on the gain. Real estate transfer tax applies to a deed that conveys Iowa real estate when the consideration exceeds $500, at 80 cents for each $500 or fractional part above $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1). The full price counts as consideration, including any lien the buyer assumes.

  • A declaration of value, signed by at least one buyer or seller, goes to the county recorder with the deed.
  • Personal property is presumed part of the price unless its value is stated on the instrument.
  • Property tax on Iowa homes runs a year behind and is billed in September and March.
  • A seller closing from July 1 to December 31 owes the September installment, and one closing from January 1 to June 30 owes the March one.

An as-is cash sale leaves these rules unchanged. What changes is who pays for repairs and how fast the deal closes. Before you sign, ask the title company to list each tax and fee that will come out of your proceeds, and talk with a tax preparer about the gain itself.

faqs.q: Is there a capital gains tax in Iowa?
faqs.a: Iowa has no separate capital gains tax. Gains are part of Iowa taxable income, which is taxed at a flat 3.8 percent for tax year 2026.

faqs.q: Do I pay Iowa tax on the sale of my primary residence?
faqs.a: Only on gain above the exclusion. Iowa generally follows the federal rule that lets you exclude up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you meet the ownership and use tests.

faqs.q: Can I deduct capital gains on a rental house sold in Iowa?
faqs.a: Not under the old non-farm real property deduction. It was repealed for tax years starting January 1, 2023, apart from installment sales begun before then.

faqs.q: Does Iowa tax gain when I inherit and sell a house?
faqs.a: Gain is measured from the stepped-up basis, usually the fair market value at the date of death. If you sell at about that value, little gain results.

faqs.q: Do I owe Iowa tax if I sold an Iowa house after moving out of state?
faqs.a: Possibly. Gain on Iowa property is Iowa-source income, and a nonresident must file when Iowa-source net income is $1,000 or more.
